name: Pompe Disease

prevalence.estimate: 1 in 40,000 (combined infantile and late-onset); infantile-onset ~1 in 138,000

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: ACMG and expert consensus guidelines for Pompe disease diagnosis

criteria.description: Deficient acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) enzyme activity in dried blood spot (DBS), leukocytes, or fibroblasts
Biallelic pathogenic variants in GAA gene
Muscle biopsy showing vacuolar myopathy with glycogen accumulation and acid phosphatase reactivity
Clinical features consistent with infantile-onset (cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, respiratory failure) or late-onset (proximal myopathy, respiratory insufficiency) Pompe disease

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Deficient GAA enzyme activity confirmed in two separate sample types (e.g., DBS confirmed in leukocytes or fibroblasts) or GAA enzyme deficiency plus biallelic GAA mutations
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (IOPD) presents before age 12 months with cardiomyopathy and is fatal within 1-2 years without treatment. Late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) presents from childhood to adulthood with limb-girdle weakness and respiratory insufficiency without significant cardiomyopathy. Newborn screening is expanding globally.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with generalized hypotonia in infant (infantile-onset)
pathognomonic.notes: Massive cardiomegaly in IOPD; typically absent in LOPD

common.notes: Lower limbs and trunk affected earlier than upper limbs; Gowers sign may be present
Disproportionate to limb weakness; may present as sleep-disordered breathing or respiratory failure. May be presenting feature in LOPD.
Infantile-onset; profound generalized hypotonia with head lag and frog-leg posture

common.symptomName: Feeding difficulties and failure to thrive (IOPD)

occasional.notes: Common in LOPD; paraspinal and abdominal wall weakness
May precede daytime respiratory symptoms in LOPD

rare.notes: Glycogen accumulation in vascular smooth muscle; basilar artery aneurysm reported

laboratory: Deficient acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) enzyme activity (DBS, leukocytes, or fibroblasts)
Elevated creatine kinase (CK) - typically 2-10x normal in LOPD; higher in IOPD
Elevated urine glucose tetrasaccharide (Hex4) - useful for monitoring treatment response
Elevated serum AST and ALT (muscle origin)
imaging: Chest X-ray / echocardiography showing massive cardiomegaly in IOPD
Muscle MRI showing fatty infiltration of paraspinal, gluteal, and thigh muscles (LOPD)
CT/MRI of diaphragm showing diaphragmatic thinning
Chest CT showing basilar atelectasis from diaphragmatic weakness
genetic: Biallelic pathogenic variants in GAA gene (chromosome 17q25.3)
IVS1-13T>G (c.-32-13T>G) is the most common mutation in late-onset Caucasian patients
Severe mutations (nonsense, large deletions) cause infantile-onset disease
Genotype-phenotype correlation: residual enzyme activity predicts severity
other: Pulmonary function testing showing restrictive pattern with reduced FVC (supine FVC drop >10% suggests diaphragmatic weakness)
EMG showing myopathic pattern with fibrillation potentials and myotonic discharges (especially paraspinal)
Muscle biopsy: vacuolar myopathy with PAS-positive glycogen accumulation, acid phosphatase-positive vacuoles
Newborn screening via DBS GAA enzyme assay (expanding internationally)

distinguishingFeatures: LGMD lacks significant respiratory involvement relative to limb weakness (in most subtypes)
Normal GAA enzyme activity in LGMD
Specific genetic mutations for each LGMD subtype
Polymyositis has elevated inflammatory markers and autoantibodies
Muscle biopsy shows inflammatory infiltrate rather than vacuolar myopathy
SMA is a motor neuron disease with denervation pattern on EMG
CK normal or mildly elevated in SMA
MG has fatigable weakness with ptosis and diplopia
MG has anti-AChR or anti-MuSK antibodies
EMG shows decremental response in MG
McArdle disease (GSD V) has exercise-induced cramps and myoglobinuria
GSD III (Cori/Forbes) has hepatomegaly with fasting hypoglycemia
Different enzyme deficiencies and genetic causes

redFlags: Infantile-onset with massive cardiomegaly and hypotonia (emergency: initiate ERT immediately)
Unexplained respiratory failure requiring ventilator support (test for LOPD)
Elevated CK with limb-girdle weakness and disproportionate respiratory involvement
Anti-rhGAA antibody development reducing ERT efficacy (especially in CRIM-negative IOPD)
Rapidly progressive respiratory decline in treated patients (assess ERT response and antibody status)
references: Kishnani PS, et al. Pompe disease diagnosis and management guideline. Genet Med. 2006;8(5):267-88.

Toscano A, Rodolico C, Musumeci O. Multisystem late onset Pompe disease (LOPD): an update on clinical aspects. Ann Transl Med. 2019;7(13):284.
Lim JA, Li L, Raben N. Pompe disease: from pathophysiology to therapy and back again. Front Aging Neurosci. 2014;6:177.
